newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan industry, bourses forsake Islamic weekend.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan industry, bourses forsake Islamic weekend.

text.p: Pakistan stock exchanges and industrialists on Friday worked through the traditional Islamic holiday adopted 20 years ago, facing only small protests from orthodox Moslems and business community critics.

Witnesses said about 200 members of a religious party protested in front of the Karachi Stock Exchange (KSE) as it opened for business after deciding to switch to a Saturday-Sunday weekend from the Friday-Saturday weekend.
The KSE closed its gates while the protesters chanted slogans against doing business on a Moslem holy day.
The Karachi bourse tumbled in early trade, but brokers said the decision to switch back to a Saturday-Sunday weekend will be good in the long run.

The national organisation of trade and industry decided last month to observe the weekly holiday on Sunday from October 6 onwards. They had switched to Fridays 20 years ago on orders issued to appease Moslem clergy by then-prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto.

His daughter, present Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto, has sidestepped demands for an official switchover to a Sunday holiday, fearing a backlash from the orthodox clergy, most of whom already opposes her government.

The Federation of Pakistan Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FPCCI) says the Islamic weekend on Friday was harmful to trade because most of the rest of world remains open on Friday and closes on Saturday and Sunday, when Pakistan used to be open.
That arrangement effectively cut off Pakistani traders from Europe for three days and from the United States for three and a half days because of the time difference, FPCCI officials said.
The KSE, Pakistan's exchanges in Lahore and Islamabad and several other trading groups have backed the FPCCI decision.

But groups of smaller traders have opposed the move, calling it arbitary and accusing the FPCCI, whose is leadership is dominated by big business, of trying to impose its will on small traders and the general population.

There were not many clients when the KSE opened for trading on Friday and volumes were low. But eventually the decision would pay off as now Pakistan will work on the day when all the international markets are open, dealer Khalid Hussain said.
"We hope the banks will also follow suit, which will be good for the trading."
All government officies, banks, financial institutions, shops and markets still observe Friday as a holiday.
"It will be good for the Pakistani business and industry if the government officially declares Friday as a working day instead of Sunday," dealer Ali Asghar of Fortune Securities said.
But dealers said the fear of a backlash from Islamist groups is keeping the government from making a similar switchover.
"The government seems to be waiting to see how people react to the decision of business and industry about making Friday a working day," dealer Mudassar Malik said.
No immediate government comment was available.
The KSE said trading hours on Friday will be from 0500 to 0715 GMT, about two hours less than the normal trading hours to allow members and staff to attend Friday prayers.
